title: Error surface over step and method: which method wins where?
summary: A colour map of the global error as a function of step size (across) and method (down). Stars mark the method with the smallest error at each step size, so the map shows where a higher-order method really pays off.

media.alt: Heat map of global error on a log colour scale: rows are Euler, Heun, RK3, RK4, RK6, RK8; columns are step sizes from 1e-3 to 1; colour moves from yellow (tiny error) at the top left to dark purple at the right; stars mark the best method at each h.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which method wins where?
read_the_figure.axes: x: step size h, logarithmic (1e-3 to 1). y: a categorical axis of methods ordered by order (Euler p = 1 up to RK8 p = 8). Colour: global error on a logarithmic scale from 1e-16 to 1.
look_at: Does colour darken to the right (larger h, larger error) in every row?
Which row is brightest at the left edge, and how large is the gap between rows there?
Where do the stars change row, and what does that say about the largest useful step for each method?
What is the colour scale clipped at (1e-16 here), and are any cells saturated?
as_drawn: Six methods of order 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 with the synthetic error C h^p (constants 1, 2, 6, 25, 300, 5000), clipped below at 1e-16, with a little multiplicative noise.
Stars run along the RK8 row for h up to about 0.25, then jump to RK3 near h = 0.3, to Heun near 0.35 to 0.4 and to Euler for h above 0.5; no star ever sits on RK4 or RK6.
The colour scale is viridis reversed, so bright yellow is small error; the colour bar is labelled global error (log scale) with ticks every two decades.
The stars use the same h for every method, so the map says nothing about cost: RK8 needs several times more function evaluations per step than Euler.
read_the_figure.proves: The map shows which method gives the smallest error at each step size. It is one honest way to see that high order only wins when h is small enough, and that the order of a method decides how fast the colour changes along its row.
if_wrong: Stars on a high-order row at large h: the error model is wrong there; stability or the non-asymptotic range changes the ranking.
A uniformly saturated yellow region: the clip level has been reached; there the colour carries no information.
Cost not shown: concluding that RK8 is best is premature until the work per step is accounted for.
must_check: log colour scale: errors span sixteen decades, so a linear colour scale would show only the largest values.

terms.meaning: The error at a fixed final time after integrating the whole interval with a given method and step.
The factor C in e = C h^p; it depends on the method and on the problem.
The exponent of h in the error. RK4 has p = 4, RK8 has p = 8.
A colour map where equal colour steps are equal error ratios, not equal differences.
An axis of named items (here methods) with no numerical spacing; the order of the rows is a choice.

remember: e = C h^p: a higher p wins only below a crossover h.
Crossover between orders p1 < p2: h* = (C2 / C1)^(1/(p1 - p2)).
Colour changes faster along a high-order row.
Stars compare at equal h, not at equal cost.
The scale is clipped at the floor: do not read bright yellow as exact.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is the step size and each row is one method, so the picture is a table of errors laid out spatially. The colour of each cell encodes the error on a logarithmic scale; a star marks the smallest value in each column. The row labels carry the order p so the reader can relate the rate of change along a row to the label.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: you are comparing many methods at many step sizes, which would be a long table. Colour turns the table into a picture where a vertical scan at one h shows which method is brightest, and a horizontal scan along a row shows how fast one method improves. The stars remove the need to scan at all.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Equal h is not equal cost: a method of order 8 needs more stages, so a star on RK8 at h = 0.1 hides that Euler could have used ten times the steps for the same work. Colour is a weak channel for quantities that differ by one decade, so subtle gaps between neighbouring rows are hard to read. A clipped floor makes the lowest cells look equal when they are not. And the map reflects one problem: a stiff problem would reverse the picture because of stability.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A work-precision diagram (F5.9) puts cost on an axis and compares at equal cost, which is the fair comparison. Line plots of error against h (F5.1) show the slope directly. For many methods, a rank plot or the crossover step in a table can be clearer.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace h by cost per unit time on the x axis, mark the stability limit of each method with a vertical tick in its row, and overlay a thin contour at the target accuracy.

steps.title: The error model of each row
steps.note: Each row is a straight line on a log-log plot (F5.1); here they are the values of the colour.

steps.title: Where a higher order starts to win
steps.note: For Euler (C = 1, p = 1) and Heun (C = 2, p = 2) this gives h = 0.5; Heun and RK3 (C = 6) cross at 1/3, matching the star positions in the render.

steps.title: Error of the best method at one step
steps.note: The star at each column marks the row achieving this minimum. For h = 0.01 RK8 gives 5000 x 1e-16 = 5e-13.

worked.title: Reading the best method from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which method is best at h = 0.01 and what is its error? (2) At what step size does Euler become the best method, and is that a useful step? (3) Where does Heun give way to RK3?

solution.text: (1) The star at h = 0.01 is on the RK8 row, in a green cell. Compute the model's value.
(2) Euler's row carries the stars only for h above about 0.5. At that step size the Euler error is about 0.5, which is useless accuracy for most purposes, so the star there is true but not useful.
(3) The crossover of the error curves is where C h^p are equal.
The render's stars on Heun at 0.35 and 0.41 and on RK3 at 0.29 agree to within the plotted noise.

worked.answer: RK8 at about 5e-13 for h = 0.01; Euler wins only for h of 0.5 and above, where its error is of order 0.5; Heun gives way to RK3 near h = 1/3.

analyze.q: Why do no stars appear on RK4 or RK6, and does that mean those methods are useless?
analyze.hint: The model is a constant times a power, and the crossovers are computed above.

analyze.q: What would the map look like for a stiff problem with a stability limit h < 0.05 on every explicit method?
analyze.hint: What happens to the error when the method is unstable?

analyze.q: Why is it harder to compare neighbouring rows than rows far apart?
analyze.hint: Colour discrimination on a log scale.

evaluate.q: A reviewer says RK8 is the best method because it holds the stars. Do you agree?
evaluate.hint: Cost per step and the problem.

create: Draw the same map with the x axis in function evaluations (steps times stages) and see which method now holds the stars.
Add a column at the right for the stability limit and grey out the cells beyond it.

checks.q: What does a star mean on this map?
checks.hint: What is compared and what is not?
checks.answer: It marks the method with the smallest error at that step size. It compares at equal h, not at equal cost.

checks.q: Method 1 has C = 4 and p = 2, method 2 has C = 40 and p = 4. At what h do they have equal error?
checks.answer: 4 h^2 = 40 h^4, so h^2 = 0.1 and h = 0.316; below that the order-4 method wins.

checks.q: RK8 holds all the stars for small h, but an engineer still chooses RK4. Give two honest reasons.
checks.hint: Think about cost and about the target error.
checks.answer: RK8 needs more function evaluations per step, so at equal cost RK4 can be cheaper for a modest target; also high-order methods need smooth solutions and may be limited by stability or round-off before they show their order.
